correctness.rationale: In each radial sector |theta|<=alpha, the side with largest cosine in the signed-distance formula is nearest. Along each ray sqrt-space is not needed: sinh(delta)=cot(alpha)cosh(r)-csc(alpha)cos(theta)sinh(r) decreases strictly to the geodesic boundary or ideal endpoint. On the sector edge it equals cot(alpha)e^(-r), giving the corner radius and ruling out clearance above the inradius. The Fermi relation cosh(t)sinh(s)=sinh(r)sin(theta) then yields the side half-span log(cos(alpha)coth(t)), so coarea gives the density and the antiderivative and endpoint values normalize it. Differentiating the continuous angular-parameter formula gives the strictly positive W(t)-W(rho) factor on common support; the remainder of the order follows from the support endpoints. The pointwise limit is proper, with tail asymptotic 2e^(-t)/pi. The density difference has exactly one sign change at tanh(t)=cos(alpha)^(n/2), interior for n>2; the CDF gap there is total variation, and the logarithmic terms cancel. Expanding log cos and arcsin gives the stated two-term expansion. The square endpoint coefficient also follows from the derivative of the density at the inradius. Replay: python3 /workspace/independent_checks.py 1 checked twenty direct polar-area comparisons and independently maximized five CDF gaps. The frozen verification and checker were inspected, not executed; finite quadrature is corroboration only.

value.rationale: The nearest-side distance is a canonical observable for finite-area ideal polygons. A diverging inradius might misleadingly suggest that typical samples have diverging clearance; the complete, strictly ordered family instead has a tight nondegenerate limit, and exact total variation quantifies its approach. The contribution goes beyond tabulating one special polygon or evaluating a known endpoint coefficient.
